summary:
MarsWalker is a web tool that plans safe spacewalks on Mars. Users drop waypoints on a map of the Jezero Crater delta, and the app instantly finds the lowest-effort round-trip route from the habitat, avoiding steep slopes, rough ground, and loose dust. It then tracks oxygen and time along the route and raises a clear warning at the point of no return: the moment there is no longer enough oxygen to get back safely.

It addresses the Martian Map challenge by turning NASA Mars Trek terrain, imagery, and thermal data, accessed through its public API, into a practical survival guide: a map that shows not just where an astronaut can walk, but how far they can go and still make it back.

It matters because on Mars, every route is a safety decision. MarsWalker makes that trade-off visible, interactive, and easy to explore for mission planners, students, and space enthusiasts, on any device and with no server required.
details:
What it does

MarsWalker is a web tool that plans safe spacewalks (EVAs) on Mars. Users drop waypoints on a map of the Jezero Crater delta, and the app instantly computes the lowest-effort route from the habitat, through every waypoint, and back. It then tracks oxygen and time along the route and warns the crew at the point of no return: the moment there is no longer enough oxygen to get back to the habitat with a safety reserve.

How it works

The study area is a 2 × 2 km zone divided into a 200 × 200 grid of 10 m cells. Each cell gets a “walking cost” based on three factors: slope (steeper costs much more), terrain roughness (a proxy for rocks), and loose dust (from thermal inertia). Cells steeper than 25° are blocked. The A* pathfinding algorithm then finds the cheapest path between consecutive waypoints, and the legs are chained into a full round trip. Users can also change the initial oxygen level and the suit’s total endurance, and the whole mission budget updates instantly.

Benefits and intended impact

Mission planners, students, and space enthusiasts can explore how terrain and oxygen limit how far an astronaut can safely go. The key idea is that on Mars the question isn’t how far you can go, but how far you can go and still make it back. It makes that trade-off visible and easy to experiment with.

Data and tools

Terrain, imagery, and thermal data come from NASA Mars Trek through its WMTS API, requested directly with no downloaded image files. The app is written in plain JavaScript with Leaflet for the map, plus a Python pipeline that prepares the data. All route calculation runs in the browser, so it works as a static site hosted on GitHub Pages, with no server. The interface is responsive for desktop, tablet, and phone.

What makes it creative

Instead of just showing a map, MarsWalker turns the oxygen limit into something you can see: a large, unmistakable warning at the exact point where a mission becomes unsafe, with a marker on the map and a one-tap jump to it. Interactive waypoint placement lets anyone test “what if” scenarios in seconds.

Factors our team considered

We considered terrain safety, effort, oxygen margin, and a reserve that is never touched. We were also careful about scientific honesty. Walking speed (0.8 m/s, slowing with slope), oxygen endurance (8 h by default, editable), the 15% reserve, and 20 minutes of work per waypoint are working assumptions, not NASA measurements. They are stated in the interface and can be changed. Route quality also depends on the resolution of the elevation data used.
